hook.line: In Shakespeare’s “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” a character laments: “The nine men’s morris is filled up with mud.”
hook.say: Let me guide you through the history of morris.

ch.say: It was played all over Europe.
p: Boards have been found scratched into Roman ruins and other sites, and the game was hugely popular in medieval Europe.
Boards were carved even into church floors and cloisters, and giant boards were cut into village greens.

ch.say: Even a Viking ship carried a board!
tl: Boards scratched at Egyptian and Roman sites (dates debated)
A board carved on the Viking Gokstad ship
Recorded in Alfonso X’s Book of Games
Computer analysis shows it is a draw

ch.say: Make three in a row and take a piece!
ch.cap: 24 points on three nested squares joined by lines
p: Players first place nine pieces each in turn, then move them along the lines.
Three in a line is a “mill” — remove an enemy piece. Reduce them to two, or leave them stuck, to win.

ch.say: Siblings with different numbers of pieces.
cards: The smallest version, three pieces each
Twelve pieces on a board with diagonals; still played in tournaments

ch.say: It even appears in great literature.
cards: In “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” the game appears in a speech lamenting the ruined seasons
A Swiss researcher who examined every position and showed it is a draw

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: The nine pieces each player uses
In many rules they may “fly” to any point

ch.say: Enjoy the thrill of three in a row!
p: Bring back the cheers of the medieval square.
